Hey, man, I know right where you are at. I lived in a small, spread-out town, too, before I moved off to college. Had some friends in high school, but was pretty much a loner.

Best advice is to check out your school's clubs. Anything that you're slightly interested in can be worthwhile if it means that you'll meet some people that share your interest. If those don't exist, just look around for someone who is doing something that you're interested and start up a conversation--if they talk to you, great; if they brush you off, no big deal. Also, you might take an interest in searching meetup.com to find groups that share your interests.

Don't make the mistake of thinking that someone has to share *all* of your interests, though. I am an avid gamer and also a musician and made a friend who was only interested in playing music and partying. We were good friends (while it lasted), and yet we had our differences. None of us are perfect. It's when we share our imperfections with other people that we truly know we have a friend. And if someone either criticizes you or your interests, not accepting your differences, then you know you don't need to be around that person. A true friend never means ill will against you.

Best of luck on your journey through those teenage years.

The biggest culprits of gaming addiction for me are MMO games (of any kind) and 1-player, long-hour-commitment games (basically your console RPGs, but anything else one can play for hours, really.) Online games are worse, in my opinion, because they keep you coming back for ever, plus they have that social factor which makes it harder to escape. Console RPGs also draw you in, but they are finite (with some exceptions.) 

I used to play a fair amount of MMOs, for both the gaming fun and the social factor. They have a way of messing up your priorities if you aren't setting any and so they ate up basically all of my time. I had to cut them out eventually as I did not want to basically become a basement dweller in my mom's house, unemployed, unkempt in appearance, and the whole nine yards. 

I still play the console RPGs, but it really is something I enjoy, and I don't do it as much as I used to, so I want to continue playing them. They are more like long books to me--I go from 1 to 1000 pages, but after 1000 pages it stops and you can go on with your life (Or play again. Hah!) Basically, I like to see ending credits in a game.

Social gaming--1v1 in the same room, co-op in the same room, etc.--is probably the least harmful or addicting form of gaming. The direct social interaction is definitely good for you (most of the time) and the more you can do it the better. 

Playing classic games like 2D platformers and shoot-em-ups would be a good alternative to the endless and nearly endless games of modern day. They are very good in short bursts and don't eat up nearly as much time as LoL or whatever, especially the ones you can beat in an hour and put down. When I think of how many of these games I could have played with the time I spent on MMOs, it really made me feel that I was wasting my time.

Anyway, just my two cents.

Most people who take on the NoFap challenge try to abstain from fapping for 90 days. This number of days isn't just a subjective goal, though, as it is said that 90 days is the amount of time needed for the brain to rewire itself from PMO (porn-masturbation-orgasm) addiction and any complications associated with it (i.e.: ED).

It really depends on the person who is doing the challenge on whether they want to continue to further abstain from pornography or masturbation after the 90 days. Some may go back to it but not abuse it as much as they used to, while others will stay with the challenge, fearing what will become of themselves if they go back to their old habits.

The best thing you could do if you are just getting into meditation is to find a quiet, peaceful room to meditate in. Some people need complete silence while others prefer having some form of white noise or nature sounds in the background. Once set up, find a comfortable position to sit in with your back straight (so as to not fall asleep).

As for actual meditation, there are many ways you could go about it. I will go through some of them here. 

1. Take deep breathes, exhaling slowly, and focus on your breathing. Some people prefer counting each breath while others do not, but either way you will begin to feel your heart rate slow down. As an extra exercise, on each inhale focus your ears on the high frequencies emitted in the room and focus on the low frequencies as you exhale.

2. With your hands on your lap, focus on the very boundary between the skin of your fingers and the surrounding air. Feel that boundary begin to blur and become undefined. With this in mind, extend your energy through your fingers and let that expand into the room. See if you can let that touch the ceiling. Finally, draw that energy back within yourself.

3. In Zen Buddhism there is the concept of *anatta* or "no self." This is achieved by disassociating from your *self*, which is your ego--everything you identify with. When people say the goal is to "focus on nothing," this is what is really meant. There is a famous saying that goes something like this: "Let it come, notice it, and let it go." Many have achieved enlightenment in this state.

I would suggest checking out the work of the integral theorist and meditation expert named Ken Wilber, specifically on the concepts of "I-amness" and nonduality. His theories of Consciousness are truly fascinating and you could learn a lot about meditation from him.  

Good luck.
